title: A mercy to the worlds
hookLine: We sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds (21:107)
carry: the dog at the well counts

lines: ONE LINE FOR A WHOLE MISSION.
cards: For most of this surah, the prophets pass by one at a time. Ibrahim in the fire. Lut.
Nuh. Dawud and Sulayman. Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Maryam.

The surah is named for them: Al-Anbiya, the Prophets. Then, near the end, the camera turns. It looks straight at the one hearing the surah first, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and sums up his whole mission in one line.

teach.b: Verse one hundred seven. Pickthall: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples." In Arabic, rahmatan lil-'alamin: a mercy for the worlds.

teach.h: 'ALAMIN: THE SAME WORD AS PAGE ONE.
teach.b: That last word, 'alamin, is the one from the Qur'an's very first page: praise belongs to God, Lord of the 'alamin, Lord of the Worlds. Pickthall translates it peoples here, and worlds there. Both are fair.
Some commentators say it reaches past people: humans, jinn, animals, everything that is. And notice the shape: not save as, only as. The verse doesn't call mercy one part of his mission among others.
It says he was sent only as mercy. There's a hadith in Muslim's collection. Once, he was asked to curse the idolaters who opposed him.
He said he was not sent to curse; he was sent as a mercy. And the mercy keeps reaching past people.

teach.h: WATER FOR A DOG AT THE WELL.
teach.b: Bukhari records his story of a man, desperately thirsty himself, who climbed down into a well, filled his shoe with water and gave it to a dog panting at the edge, and God forgave him.
The companions asked, is there reward even for animals? He said, in every living, breathing thing there is reward. So a mercy to the worlds isn't only a title.
It sets a standard for anyone who follows him: the dog at the well counts. The ant counts. The stranger counts.

how: Muslims often quote 21:107 when describing the Prophet's character, and stories of his kindness to animals, like the man who gave water to a dog, are often taught to children.

o: a blessing meant for the Prophet's own city only
the Lord of the Worlds, a name for God alone
a mercy to the worlds: the Prophet's whole mission

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: gave water to a thirsty dog

s: 'alamin in 21:107 is the same word as in Lord of the Worlds
the same word from al-Fatiha. Pickthall renders it peoples here and worlds there.
the Prophet agreed to curse the idolaters when asked
Muslim records him saying he was not sent to curse, but as a mercy.
in the hadith, kindness to animals earns no reward
asked about animals, he said there is reward in every living thing.

games.q: you're desperately thirsty. you climb down a well and drink. back at the top, a dog is panting, licking the damp ground. what do you do?
o: walk on. you've had your water.
go back down, fill your shoe, and carry water up.
wave someone else over to help it.
games.why: he climbed back down and carried water up in his shoe, and God forgave him for it. Bukhari records the story.

practice: Look around your day for one living thing you could ease: a plant that needs water, a bird that would take a dish of it, a pet that wants your attention, a person who's been short with you.
Choose one, and picture easing it, slowly, in detail. If you pray, you can ask to be a little more like the one sent as a mercy.

wordCard.voice: Rahmatan lil-'alamin. A mercy to the worlds: the Prophet's whole mission in one line, reaching people, animals and everything that is.

carryVoice: Your line: the dog at the well counts. Mercy reaches every living, breathing thing. Until tomorrow.
